content.text:
Der Plan passt gut zu dem, was wir besprochen haben: ein Browser pro Agent, ein gemeinsamer Evidence Store und ein Orchestrator, der entscheidet. Drei Punkte würde ich ändern, weil sie sonst entweder Fehler oder viel Eigenbau bringen.

## 1. Der Orchestrator sollte die finale JSON nicht selbst zusammenstellen

„Erstellt finale JSON der relevanten Daten" heißt: Ein Modell entscheidet, was relevant ist. Damit wandern die Regel-Entscheidungen wieder ins Modell, und genau da passieren die Fehler. Ein Beispiel aus dem Opus-Benchmark: Die gültige Rabattfreigabe hat eine Mindestbestellwert-Bedingung von 1,00 €, die wie ein Fehler aussieht, und daneben steht ein Entwurf mit 99 % als Köder. Ein Modell, das „relevante Daten" auswählt, kann da leicht falsch filtern.

**Besser:** Die finale JSON ist einfach der Snapshot des Stores, also alle Belege inklusive der Köder. Was davon gilt, entscheidet `resolve()` deterministisch. Der Orchestrator entscheidet nur, *wann* die Suche fertig ist, und zwar anhand von `open_questions()`: offene Lücken aus den Regeln plus Abdeckung (z. B. „Q&A-Seiten 5–6 noch nicht gelesen"), nicht nach Gefühl.

## 2. Die Browser-Agenten sollten nicht durchgehend laufen, sondern pro Auftrag

Dauerhaft laufende Agenten, die Kommandos empfangen, bedeuten Eigenbau: Warteschlangen, Nachrichten an laufende Prozesse, Keep-alive. Genau das zu niedrige Level, das du vermeiden willst. Dazu kommt: Ihr Kontext wächst über den ganzen Lauf, was jeden weiteren Aufruf langsamer und teurer macht.

**Besser:** Jeder Auftrag ist ein eigener Agent-Aufruf, der an Browser N gebunden ist und fertig zurückkommt. Das Gedächtnis liegt nicht im Agenten, sondern
- **im Browser**, der zwischen den Aufträgen eingeloggt bleibt, mit Tabs und Cookies,
- **im Store**, der alle Funde enthält.

Das ist genau das Subagent-Modell von Claude Code: Der Orchestrator schickt „Browser 3: Durchsuche das ERP nach Kataloggruppe G-1" los und bekommt eine Zeile Status zurück. Ein neuer Auftrag startet mit frischem, kleinem Kontext. Bei Session-Timeouts (das ERP hat einen kurzen) loggt sich der nächste Auftrag einfach neu ein.

## 3. Browser als freie Slots, nicht fest einer Website zugeordnet

„4 Browser-Agenten" klingt nach einem Agenten pro Website. Die Arbeit ist aber ungleich verteilt: Das ERP braucht viele Kandidaten-Prüfungen, und der Tender-Agent ist früher fertig. Im privaten Datensatz sind die Infos laut Brief außerdem anders auf die Seiten verteilt.

**Besser:** 4 Browser-Slots. Der Orchestrator gibt jeden Auftrag an einen freien Browser, auch zwei gleichzeitig ans ERP, wenn dort am meisten offen ist.

## Kleinigkeiten
- **Die Browser-Agenten lesen selbst aus dem Store** (`query`, `wait_for`). Der ERP-Agent holt sich die Kataloggruppen also direkt, statt dass der Orchestrator alles weiterreichen muss.
- **Die Abgabe fehlt im Plan noch.** Nach der Retrieval-Phase kommen `resolve()` und `pricing.py`, die das Gebot berechnen, und danach ein Auftrag „Gebot eingeben und signieren" an zwei Browser: Tender-Portal und Mail.

## Überarbeitet

> **Ziel:** Die Retrieval-Agenten füllen einen Evidence Store. Dessen Snapshot ist die JSON, die `resolve()` liest.
> **Orchestrator:** liest den Store und `open_questions()`, vergibt Aufträge an freie Browser-Slots und erklärt die Suche für beendet, wenn keine Fragen mehr offen sind.
> **Browser-Agenten:** ein Auftrag pro Aufruf, an einen Browser gebunden. Sie schreiben Belege in den Store, sobald sie etwas finden, und geben eine Zeile Status zurück.
> **Danach:** `resolve()` + `pricing.py` → Gebot → Abgabe-Agent.

Damit bleibt eure Arbeit auf der richtigen Ebene: Store-Server, Prompts, Subagent-Definitionen. Die Agent-Schleifen übernimmt Claude Code.

content.text:
`resolve()` ist der **Sachbearbeiter mit dem Regelbuch**. Die Browser-Agenten legen ihm einen Stapel Belege auf den Tisch, also alles, was sie gefunden haben, auch Veraltetes und Köder. `resolve()` geht den Stapel nach den Regeln aus dem Brief durch und sagt am Ende: „Das ist das Gebot." Es ist reiner Python-Code, ohne KI. Gleicher Stapel bedeutet immer gleiches Ergebnis.

## Was rein- und rausgeht

**Rein:** die Evidence-JSON aus dem Store, zum Beispiel:
```
Rabatt-Mails:  03-01  leitung@   AB-1000    6 %
               03-08  leitung@   AB-1000    8 %
               03-09  leitung@   AB-1000-A  15 %
               03-12  leitung@   AB-1000    20 %
               03-04  vertrieb@  AB-1000    30 %
```

**Raus:** das fertige Gebot im Format, das Atira erwartet, plus eine Begründung, welcher Beleg was entschieden hat.

## Was es macht, in drei Schritten

**1. Aussortieren, was nicht gilt.** Die Regeln aus dem Brief, als Code:
- 15 %: falsche Referenz (AB-1000**-A**) → raus
- 20 %: nach dem Stichtag 03-10 → raus
- 30 %: falscher Absender (vertrieb@ statt leitung@) → raus
- zurückgezogene Q&A-Antworten → raus
- Revisionen, die nicht als „aktuell" markiert sind → raus

**2. Unter dem Rest das Gültige auswählen.**
- Von 6 % und 8 % gilt die **neueste** Freigabe → **8 %**.
- Für jede Position die passende Anforderung, die neueste Mengenänderung, ein aktives Material, das in allen fünf Merkmalen exakt passt, und den Preis, der am Stichtag gilt.

**3. Rechnen.** Mit `pricing.py`: Staffelpreis, Rabatt, Zuschläge, Verpackung, Rüstkosten, Bonus und Summe, mit kaufmännischer Rundung genau an den Stellen, die der Brief vorschreibt.

## Was passiert, wenn ein Beleg fehlt

Dann rechnet es nicht falsch weiter, sondern meldet eine **offene Frage**, z. B.:

> „Position 1 braucht den Metallindex MET-1. Bitte in der Mail bei kalkulation@ suchen."

Das ist `open_questions()`: dieselbe Funktion, nur dass man auf die Lücken schaut statt aufs Gebot. Daran sieht der Orchestrator, was die Browser-Agenten noch suchen müssen und wann die Suche fertig ist.

## Die Arbeitsteilung

| | Wer | Warum |
|---|---|---|
| **Finden**: wo suchen, was ist ein relevanter Beleg | Browser-Agenten (KI) | Websites sind unübersichtlich und verändern sich, dafür braucht man ein Modell |
| **Entscheiden und Rechnen**: welcher Beleg gilt, welcher Preis | `resolve()` (Code) | Die Regeln sind fest. Code macht dabei nie Fehler, ein Modell manchmal schon |

Kurz gesagt: Die KI sammelt, `resolve()` wendet die Regeln an und rechnet.

- **`compute_bid()`**: Am Ende kommt das fertige Gebot heraus.

Der Orchestrator ruft also ein Tool auf, das Skript läuft in Millisekunden und gibt das Ergebnis zurück. In der Architektur bleibt es bei **5 Agenten** (Orchestrator plus 4 Browser-Agenten). `resolve()` ist kein sechster, sondern ein Rechenwerkzeug, das sie benutzen.

Resolve doesn't need to be "smart" so much as complete — it just has to faithfully implement the fixed, explicit rulebook of 28 rules (plus the private dataset), which is careful engineering rather than intelligence.

Interpretation of prose into structured fields (scope enums, date formats, approval detection) happens upstream in the extraction agents, so resolve just handles mechanics. The real risk is edge cases the rules don't cover or missing schema fields — mitigated by per-rule tests, warnings, and the Opus benchmark, which ran this exact resolver end-to-end on public-1 with no gaps and a full 5/5 bid.

As for iteration: resolve itself is stateless and recomputes everything from scratch each call since it's cheap; the actual iteration lives in the orchestrator loop, which keeps calling resolve to find gaps, assigns tasks to agents, and repeats until nothing's missing before computing the bid.

content.text:
Zwei Fragen: Wie schlau muss `resolve()` sein, und läuft das iterativ?

## Muss `resolve()` sehr schlau sein?

Nicht schlau, sondern **vollständig**. Die Regeln stehen alle ausdrücklich im Brief, 28 Stück, und der Brief sagt, dass sie im privaten Datensatz dieselben sind. `resolve()` setzt also ein bekanntes Regelwerk sorgfältig um, z. B. „neueste Freigabe von leitung@ für exakt diese Referenz, nicht nach dem Stichtag". Das ist Fleißarbeit, keine Intelligenz.

**Das Schlaue passiert vorher, bei den Agenten.** Alles, was Verständnis braucht, übersetzen sie beim Speichern in feste Felder:

| Auf der Website | Was der Agent speichert | Was `resolve()` damit macht |
|---|---|---|
| „Waren-Grundpreis und Materialteuerung bilden die rabattfähige Basis" | `scope: "base_and_surcharge"` | Rabatt auf Grundpreis und Zuschlag |
| „01/17 (MM/TT) 2027" | `date: "2027-01-17"` | Datum vergleichen |
| „Bitte prüfen Sie … Dies ist keine Rabattfreigabe." | `kind: "other"` | ignorieren |

Die Agenten **verstehen** also Text, `resolve()` **wendet Regeln an**.

**Das Risiko:** Ein Fall, den der Code nicht abdeckt, oder ein Feld, das im Schema fehlt. Dagegen helfen die Tests pro Regel, die Warnungen, und vor allem der Vergleich mit dem Opus-Benchmark. Der hat genau diesen Weg schon genommen, Evidence-JSON → `resolve()` → Gebot, und auf public-1 ein vollständiges Gebot ergeben: 5 von 5 Positionen, keine Lücken, keine Warnungen. Ob alle Werte stimmen, zeigt erst ein bewerteter Testlauf.

## Läuft das iterativ?

Ja, aber **die Wiederholung macht der Orchestrator, nicht `resolve()`**. `resolve()` hat kein Gedächtnis. Jeder Aufruf rechnet den ganzen aktuellen Store von vorn durch. Weil das Millisekunden dauert, kann man es beliebig oft aufrufen:

| Runde | Im Store | `open_questions()` sagt | Orchestrator schickt |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | leer | „Positionen erfassen" | 4 Agenten: Tender, Spec, ERP, Mail |
| 2 | Positionen, Q&A, Revisionen | „ERP nach G-1 und G-2 durchsuchen" | ERP-Agent (läuft evtl. schon) |
| 3 | + Materialien | „Metallindex MET-1 fehlt" | Mail-Agent: gezielt danach suchen |
| 4 | + Metallindex | keine Lücken mehr | → `compute_bid()` → Gebot |

Bei jedem Aufruf geht es also so: Store-Snapshot (JSON) → `resolve()` → entweder Lücken (weiter suchen) oder ein fertiges Gebot. Der Kreislauf läuft über die Agenten: Sie füllen den Store, `resolve()` prüft, der Orchestrator schickt die nächsten Aufträge, bis nichts mehr fehlt.

Ich will die Begriffe klären: "Agent" bedeutet ein LLM in einer Schleife mit Tools, während ein "einfacher LLM-Aufruf" eine einzelne Frage-Antwort-Interaktion ist — im Kern besteht jeder Agent aus vielen solchen Einzelaufrufen, die Claude Code zu einer Schleife verbindet. content.text:
Alle fünf sind **Claude Code**: eine einzige Claude-Code-Sitzung (`claude -p`) mit Subagenten.

| Agent | Was er technisch ist | Modell (Vorschlag) |
|---|---|---|
| **Orchestrator** | die Haupt-Sitzung von Claude Code | Opus oder Sonnet: plant, macht aber wenige Schritte |
| **4 Browser-Agenten** | Subagenten von Claude Code, über das Agent-Tool gestartet, jeder mit seinem eigenen Browser | Sonnet oder Haiku: viele Klicks, also lieber schnell und günstig |

Das Modell lässt sich pro Subagent in seiner Definition festlegen.

**Warum keine einfachen LLM-Calls?** Ein einfacher Call ist eine Frage und eine Antwort. Browsen braucht dagegen eine **Schleife**: klicken, Ergebnis ansehen, nächsten Schritt entscheiden, wieder klicken, oft 20 bis 80 Mal pro Website. Auch der Orchestrator braucht eine Schleife: Agenten starten, offene Fragen prüfen, neue Aufträge vergeben. Genau diese Schleife ist ein Agent. Unter der Haube besteht jeder Agent aus vielen einfachen LLM-Calls, aber Claude Code baut die Schleife darum: Tool-Aufrufe, Wiederholungen, Kontext-Verwaltung. Die bauen wir nicht selbst.

**Wo einfache LLM-Calls trotzdem passen:** in kleinen Hilfswerkzeugen ohne Schleife. Zum Beispiel ein optionales Tool `extract`, das eine geöffnete Seite einmal in Evidence-Records übersetzt. Das wäre ein einzelner günstiger Call, z. B. mit Haiku oder dem kostenlosen Qwen, damit die Browser-Agenten keine riesigen Seiten lesen müssen.

Im Überblick:

```
claude -p  (Orchestrator, Claude Code)
 ├─ Subagent Browser 1   ┐
 ├─ Subagent Browser 2   │  Claude Code, je eigene Schleife
 ├─ Subagent Browser 3   │
 ├─ Subagent Browser 4   ┘
 └─ Tools: Evidence Store → resolve() / compute_bid()   (Python, keine KI)
```

Lokal läuft das über dein Claude-Login. Im Atira-Sandbox über OpenRouter, so wie es der andere Thread schon für `cc-agent/` eingerichtet hat.

content.thinking:
I'm working through the user's example about an agent discovering a pointer like "this info is in A5" — recognizing this as a navigation hint rather than something resolve can handle directly, since only the orchestrator can dispatch a lookup. I'm thinking through two cases: when the schema already has a structured field like position.requirement_id to capture this kind of reference cleanly.

content.text:
Guter Punkt. Es gibt zwei Fälle, und nur einer davon kann `resolve()` selbst erkennen.

## Fall 1: Der Hinweis ist ein Feld, das die Regeln brauchen. Das erkennt `resolve()`.

Dein Beispiel ist genau so ein Fall. Der Tender-Agent liest „Position 01.05, gemäß Lastenheft Anforderung A-5" und schreibt:

```json
{"position": "01.05", "quantity": 22, "unit_kind": "set", "requirement_id": "A-5"}
```

Damit steht im Store, dass Position 01.05 die Anforderung A-5 braucht. Ruft der Orchestrator jetzt `open_questions()` auf, merkt `resolve()`, dass A-5 im Store fehlt, und meldet:

> `[customer-portal] Record requirement A-5 of revision R-… with all attributes and its Kataloggruppe.`

Der Orchestrator muss also nicht selbst verstehen, dass jemand A-5 nachschauen muss. Er bekommt die Frage fertig und schickt sie an einen freien Browser-Agenten. Dasselbe gilt für alles, was das Schema als Feld kennt: Kataloggruppen (→ „ERP durchsuchen"), Schlüssel wie K-…, VP-… oder TZ-… (→ „Mail suchen"), Metallindex-Codes, FX-Schlüssel. Jede Referenz zwischen den Belegen erzeugt eine Lücke, solange ihr Gegenstück fehlt.

## Fall 2: Ein freier Hinweis, kein Regel-Feld. Da hast du recht, das muss der Orchestrator machen.

Beispiele:
- „Stück je Satz steht im technischen Datenblatt, nicht im Viewer"
- „Ältere Mails nur über die Archivsuche sichtbar"
- „Q&A hat 6 Seiten, gelesen bis Seite 4"

Damit kann `resolve()` nichts anfangen; das sind Wegbeschreibungen, keine Daten für eine Regel. **Aktuell hat das Schema dafür nur `notes: list[str]`**, freien Text ohne Struktur. Das ist zu schwach. Ich würde einen eigenen Record-Typ ergänzen:

```json
{"id": "lead-7", "about": "Stück je Satz für A-5",
 "where": "technisches Datenblatt im Lieferantenportal",
 "found_by": "spec", "status": "open"}
```

- `resolve()` ignoriert diese Leads für die Berechnung.
- Der **Orchestrator** liest offene Leads, schickt einen Agenten los und setzt den Lead danach auf `done`.
- Andere Agenten können Leads auch selbst lesen und mitnehmen.

## Die To-do-Liste des Orchestrators

| Quelle | Woher | Beispiel |
|---|---|---|
| **Lücken** | `resolve()`: „die Regeln brauchen X, X fehlt" | „Anforderung A-5 erfassen" |
| **Leads** | Agenten: „X steht vermutlich dort" | „Stück je Satz im Datenblatt" |

Oft greifen beide ineinander. Die Lücke sagt **was** fehlt („Stück je Satz für A-5"), der Lead sagt **wo** man es findet („im Datenblatt"). Der Orchestrator verbindet beides zu einem Auftrag: „Browser 2: Öffne das Datenblatt im Lieferantenportal und speichere die Stück je Satz für A-5."

Soll ich den Lead-Typ und die Abfrage „offene Leads" in `evidence.py` ergänzen? Die Datei wurde zwischendurch von woanders geändert, das würde ich vorher prüfen.

content.text:
Yes. The relations need to be **part of the Pydantic format itself**, not only knowledge hidden in `resolve()`. Then generic code can find every broken link, the orchestrator gets a precise to-do list, and the rules stay in `resolve()`. Here's how I'd model it, in four building blocks.

## 1. Records are nodes, reference fields are edges

The current schema already has the links; they just aren't declared as links. The evidence is a graph:

```
TenderPosition.requirement_id     ──► Requirement.id          (spec)
Requirement.catalog_group         ──► ErpSearch.catalog_group ──► Material.number   (ERP)
Requirement.end_reserve_key       ──► TechnicalRelease.key    (mail, technik@)
Assignment.condition_group        ──► ConditionRule.key       (mail, kalkulation@)
Assignment.packaging_tariff       ──► PackagingTariff.key     (mail, logistik@)
Assignment.delivery_commitment    ──► DeliveryCommitment.key  ──► Material.number
Assignment.setup_pool / bonus_plan──► SetupPool.key / BonusPlan.key
Material.metal_index              ──► MetalIndexRate.code     (mail, kalkulation@)
PriceCondition.fx_key             ──► FxRate.key              (mail, finanzen@)
QAAnswer.withdraws                ──► QAAnswer.number
Amendment.revision/requirement_id ──► SpecRevision.id / Requirement.id
```

**Declare the edges in the type**, with a small marker in the field's metadata:

```python
class Ref:
    """Marks a field as a link to another record. `ask` becomes the open question when the target is missing."""
    def __init__(self, kind: str, ask: str):
        self.kind, self.ask = kind, ask

RequirementId = Annotated[str, Ref("requirement", "Record requirement {key}: all attributes, Kataloggruppe, pieces per set")]
CatalogGroup  = Annotated[str, Ref("erp_search",  "Search the ERP for Kataloggruppe {key}; open every listed material")]
MetalIndex    = Annotated[str, Ref("metal_index", "Find the Preisindizes for {key} (kalkulation@)")]

class TenderPosition(Record):
    requirement_id: RequirementId | None = None
```

**One generic function** then walks all records, reads the `Ref` markers from `model_fields[...].metadata`, and reports every link whose target doesn't exist yet:

```python
def dangling(evidence) -> list[Question]:
    index = build_index(evidence)          # {"requirement": {"A-1", ...}, "metal_index": {...}, ...}
    for record, field, ref, key in walk_refs(evidence):
        if key and key not in index[ref.kind]:
            yield Question(id=f"{ref.kind}:{key}", about=Target(kind=ref.kind, key=key),
                           text=ref.ask.format(key=key))
```

A new relation is then one annotated field, not new code in the resolver.

## 2. Two layers of checks

| Layer | Asks | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Generic: does the link exist?** | "A-5 is referenced and isn't in the store" | `dangling()`, derived from the `Ref` markers |
| **Rules: does the target apply?** | "A-5 exists, but only in a superseded revision", "the Technikfreigabe is for another revision", "the only approval is future-dated" | `resolve()` |

`open_questions()` returns both together.

## 3. Leads: "it's probably over there"

A lead points at the same kind of target as a question, so the two can be matched:

```python
class Target(Record):
    kind: str                     # "requirement", "material", "metal_index", ...
    key: str | None = None        # "A-5"
    field: str | None = None      # "pieces_per_set": only that one field is missing

class Lead(Record):
    id: str
    about: Target                 # what it's about
    where: str                    # "technical data sheet in the supplier portal"
    site: str | None = None
    found_by: str                 # which agent noted it
    status: Literal["open", "done", "dead_end"] = "open"
    answered_by: list[str] = []   # ids of the records that answered it
```

The orchestrator joins questions and leads on `Target`. Question `requirement:A-5 / pieces_per_set` plus lead "data sheet in the supplier portal" becomes the task: "Browser 2: open the data sheet, record the pieces per set for A-5."

## 4. Coverage: what's been looked at, so unknown unknowns surface too

```python
class Coverage(Record):
    id: str                       # "tender-portal:qa", "mail:archive:AB-1000 Rüstpools"
    site: str
    what: str                     # "Q&A pages", "mail search, archive folder"
    seen: int
    total: int | None = None      # None: unknown, counts as incomplete
```

`open_questions()` turns `seen < total` into "Read Q&A pages 5–6". That catches the case where a Q&A answer assigning a setup pool was simply never read, which no reference could reveal.

## What the orchestrator gets

`open_questions()` returns **typed questions with stable ids** (`requirement:A-5`, `erp_search:G-1`, `coverage:tender-portal:qa`). With stable ids:
- the store can record which question is already assigned to which browser, so nothing is dispatched twice
- a lead can be matched exactly to a question
- the orchestrator can see when a question disappears, which means it's answered

The four pieces are `Ref` markers on the existing fields, `Lead`, `Coverage`, and `Question` with the matching. Together they're roughly 100 lines in `evidence.py` and `resolver.py`. `evidence.py` was changed from somewhere else in the meantime, so I'd read the current version first and build on it. Should I?

content.text: Are these relations fixed or dynamic does a fixed format even fit this or is it more like the agent needs to figure it out

content.thinking:
I should separate what stays fixed from what varies here. The semantic relations themselves are fixed since they come from the rules — position maps to requirement, requirement maps through Kataloggruppe to ERP material, and Q&A assigns keys resolved via mails from specific senders — and these rules apply identically to the private dataset too.

What's dynamic is the physical layer: which site hosts which piece of information, how references are expressed (by name vs id), the navigation path through gates and viewers, and naming conventions like key prefixes that differ across datasets. That's the part agents need to discover, which is exactly why leads and coverage exist as unstructured "where" fields — the logical model stays fixed while the search/navigation stays flexible.

Even within a fixed schema, agents still have to resolve matching ambiguities — if a position doesn't name a requirement id but just describes a cylinder, the agent has to judge which requirement it maps to and record that link with a confidence note or quoted basis, so identity-resolution happens at write-time while the format itself never changes. I'm also thinking through escape hatches for a fixed schema: verbatim source-text fields so a reviewer can double-check, free-form leads for location data, and a generic Observation record for things that don't fit any existing type — with repeated misfits signaling a schema extension is needed later, not something agents improvise at runtime.

The crisp argument crystallizes: every fact that changes the price is named by a fixed rule, so it has a fixed slot; everything else is just navigation toward finding facts, and that's inherently dynamic, belonging to agents as leads, coverage, and free notes. I note the caveat that if the fixed relations don't match the private dataset's real structure (multiple setup pools, Satz coming from Q&A rather than spec), the resolver's assumptions could break — mitigated by surfacing gaps rather than returning silently wrong answers, and the private brief may phrase rules differently while still being "the same bid rules." Comparing this to a fully dynamic alternative — agents freely building a knowledge graph for an LLM to compute over — that approach loses determinism and reintroduces model judgment, confirming the hybrid design is the right answer; I'll respond in English, concisely, with a table.

content.text:
Both, on two different layers. A fixed format fits one layer well; the agents have to figure out the other.

## Fixed: what relates to what

Every relation that affects the price is **named by a rule in the brief**:
- position → requirement (rule 2)
- requirement → Kataloggruppe → ERP material (rule 3 and "Finding records")
- Q&A key → Konditionsregeln / tariff / commitment / pool / bonus mail from a specific sender (rules 12 and 23–26)
- material → metal index (28)
- price condition → FX key (22)
- usable stroke → Technikfreigabe for that revision (20)

The brief says the private dataset uses "the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format". So these relations stay the same. The argument in one line: **every fact that changes the answer is named by a rule, the rules are fixed, so every price-relevant fact has a fixed place in the schema.** A fixed Pydantic format fits that layer, and it's the reason `resolve()` can work at all.

## Dynamic: where things are and how they look

That's what changes between datasets, and it's what the agents figure out:

| Dynamic | Example | Who handles it |
|---|---|---|
| **Which site holds what** | Kataloggruppe in the tender documents instead of the spec; pieces per set in a data sheet or a Q&A answer | agents, recorded as **leads** |
| **How a link is expressed** | a position names its requirement by title, not by id | the agent makes the link when writing `requirement_id`, and quotes its basis in the record |
| **Names and formats** | other key prefixes, other date formats, other site names | the agent normalizes them into the fixed fields |
| **The way there** | gates, viewers, paging, archive folders | agents, recorded as **coverage** |

So the agent's real work is **linking and finding**: "this position belongs to this requirement", "that mail is the approval for this tender", "the setup fee for this position is in that Q&A answer". The format doesn't prescribe how it finds those; it only says where the result goes.

## Escape hatches, so a fixed format doesn't become a cage

1. **Verbatim text on every record** (`text`, `original_wording`). If a link is doubtful, the orchestrator or a check can reread the source.
2. **Leads with a free-text `where`** for any "it's probably over there".
3. **A free `Observation` record** for things that fit nowhere: "position 3's unit is 'VE', unknown". `resolve()` ignores it, but the orchestrator sees it. If observations keep appearing in test runs, that's a signal to **extend the schema during development**. Agents shouldn't invent new record types during a run, because `resolve()` can't use them anyway.

## The alternative, and why not

A fully dynamic format, where agents build a free-form knowledge graph and a model reads off the answer at the end, would adapt to anything. But then a model decides which records apply and calculates again, which is exactly what we moved into code. For the parts the rules cover, that only adds error risk.

## The remaining risk

The fixed layer contains a few assumptions the brief doesn't strictly guarantee: only one setup pool per order, pieces per set from the spec. If the private dataset breaks one of them, `resolve()` reports a **gap** instead of silently calculating a wrong value. That's the right failure mode, and a reason to keep the assumptions few and explicit.

content.text:
These two lines describe the chain that gets each tender position to its material number. The brief defines it in three places.

## The wording in the brief

- **Rule 2:** *"Use the requirement referenced by the position in the specification revision marked current. Superseded revisions do not apply."*
- **Rule 3:** *"Select an active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification all exactly equal that requirement. Blocked materials do not qualify. If any position has no matching active material, submit no_bid."*
- **"Finding records":** *"The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes."*

## The chain, step by step (invented values)

**1. Tender portal → position.** The bill of quantities says:
> Position 2: "Hydraulic cylinder, according to specification requirement **R-7**", 30 Stk

So position 2 points to requirement R-7. That's the first link: **position → requirement**.

**2. Spec → the right revision.** The supplier portal has three revisions of the specification. Only one is marked current (rule 2). R-7 exists in all three, with different values, so the **current** one decides:
> R-7 in REV-2 (current): bore 63, stroke 300, 250 bar, Schwenkauge, no certification, **Kataloggruppe G-2**

**3. Spec → Kataloggruppe.** That gives the second link: **requirement → Kataloggruppe G-2**. It's mainly a search key. The ERP doesn't list its whole catalogue, and empty or overly broad searches show nothing, so you have to search for G-2.

**4. ERP → candidates.** The search for G-2 lists, say, M-20, M-21 and M-22. That's the third link: **Kataloggruppe → materials**.

**5. Compare → material (rule 3).** All five attributes must be exactly equal, and the material must be active:

| Material | Bore | Stroke | Pressure | Mounting | Cert. | Status | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M-20 | 63 | 300 | 250 | Schwenkauge | none | active | **match** |
| M-21 | 63 | 300 | 250 | Schwenkauge | none | blocked | blocked, no |
| M-22 | 63 | 320 | 250 | Schwenkauge | none | active | stroke differs, no |

So position 2 gets **M-20**. If none had matched, the whole bid would be no_bid.

**Before step 5, the requirement may still change:**
- **Q&A amendments** can replace single attributes for the current revision ("Stroke for R-7 in REV-2 = 310 mm").
- **Usable stroke ("nutzbarer Weg")**: add twice the reserve from the Technikfreigabe.

The comparison uses the attributes **after** those changes.

## Who does what

| Step | Agent (finding, linking) | Code (`resolve()`) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | reads "according to requirement R-7" → `requirement_id: "R-7"` | follows the link |
| 2 | records every revision and how it's marked | picks the one marked current |
| 3 | records R-7's attributes and Kataloggruppe | applies amendments and the reserve |
| 4 | searches G-2, opens every candidate, records them, marks the search complete | — |
| 5 | — | compares the 5 attributes exactly and checks status; or decides no_bid |

This chain is fixed because rules 2 and 3 prescribe it. What varies between datasets is how each link looks on the site: whether it says "requirement R-7" or names a title, where the Kataloggruppe is printed, how the ERP search works. That part is the agents' job.

content.text:
**You can rely on the task specification for the logic, but not for clean data.** These are two different things.

## What the spec guarantees

The brief is explicit: *"These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets"*, plus *"the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format"*. The links themselves are part of those rules: position → requirement in the current revision, requirement → Kataloggruppe → active exact-match material. On the private dataset a position will still refer to a requirement, and the material will still have to match it exactly. Building the schema on that is safe.

## What it doesn't guarantee: how clean the data is

public-1 is already messy, and every case below comes from the other thread's real runs:
- **A link that contradicts itself.** Position 01.03 is called "Verstellung", but its description says "Hubwerk, according to A-2".
- **Duplicate, conflicting records.** "Weitere laden" in the spec viewer appended a second A-4 row with different values.
- **Hidden values.** The certification only appears in a tooltip; the table cell says "Prüfvermerk siehe Freigabestand".
- **Ambiguous formats.** One revision dated "11/01 (TT/MM)", another "01/17 (MM/TT)"; numbers like "200 (en-US)".
- **Values missing where you'd expect them.** Pieces per set wasn't in the spec viewer at all.
- **Decoys.** References with a "-A" suffix, a future-dated FX fixing, and a planted 99 % approval at the end of every mail.

The private dataset will likely be at least as messy, just differently.

## What can break a link, and how to design for it

| Problem | Design answer |
|---|---|
| **The link isn't stated** (the position doesn't name a requirement) | The agent may infer it, but marks it as inferred and quotes its basis. `resolve()` turns inferred links into warnings or verification questions. |
| **Sources conflict** (two A-4 rows, title vs. description) | **Keep both, don't overwrite.** `resolve()` detects the conflict and asks a targeted question ("Verify A-4 in REV-2: two different values were recorded"). |
| **Messy values** (locales, date formats, units) | The agent stores the **raw text plus the normalized value**. Code validates the normalized one; the raw one allows a recheck. |
| **Something the rules don't cover** | An `Observation` record plus a gap. You extend the schema during development, not during the run. |

**One real flaw in what I built:** `merge()` currently replaces a record when the same id arrives again. So the second A-4 row would silently overwrite the first, and the conflict would be lost. For messy data, the store should keep **every observation per id, with its source**, and let `resolve()` decide:
- **All versions agree:** fine.
- **They disagree:** don't guess. Raise a conflict question, and price nothing on that position until it's settled.

**In short:**
- **Fixed:** the rules, and so the links. Rely on the spec.
- **Assumed messy:** the data. Keep raw values and sources, treat links as explicit or inferred, keep conflicts instead of overwriting them, and have `resolve()` turn every doubt into a question instead of a guess.

content.text:
Here are the store entries for all four cases. **This is a proposed extension of `evidence.py`, not built yet.** Today's schema has no `basis`, no observation lists and no raw values. The values are invented.

Every entry gets the same envelope: `kind`, `key`, and a `source` with site, exact location, agent and time.

## 1. The link isn't stated: inferred, with its basis

The bill of quantities names no requirement for position 3. The tender agent infers one from the description:

```json
{"kind": "position", "key": "3",
 "quantity": {"raw": "16 Stk", "value": 16}, "unit_kind": "piece",
 "requirement": {
   "id": "R-2",
   "basis": "inferred",
   "quote": "Doppeltwirkender Zylinder für Hubwerk",
   "reason": "No requirement named; R-2 is the only requirement titled 'Hubwerk'"},
 "source": {"site": "tender-portal", "locator": "LV, row 3", "agent": "tender", "at": "02:14"}}
```

A stated link would just carry `"basis": "stated"` and a quote like `"gemäß Lastenheft Anforderung R-2"`.

**`resolve()` says:** it still prices position 3, but adds
- warning: `position 3: requirement R-2 is inferred, not stated`
- question `verify:position:3:requirement`: *"Position 3 names no requirement. Check the tender documents (LV file, position overview) for its requirement reference."*

## 2. Sources conflict: keep both observations

The spec agent records R-4 twice: once from its own viewer page, once from the extra row "Weitere laden" appended to page 1:

```json
{"kind": "requirement", "key": "REV-2/R-4",
 "observations": [
   {"value": {"bore_mm": 50, "stroke_mm": 576, "pressure_bar": 210, "mounting": "Schwenkauge", "certification": "none"},
    "source": {"site": "customer-portal", "locator": "viewer REV-2, page 4", "agent": "spec", "at": "03:10"}},
   {"value": {"bore_mm": 50, "stroke_mm": 600, "pressure_bar": 210, "mounting": "Schwenkauge", "certification": "none"},
    "source": {"site": "customer-portal", "locator": "viewer REV-2, page 1 after 'Weitere laden'", "agent": "spec", "at": "03:42"}}]}
```

**`resolve()` says:** positions on R-4 are **not priced** yet, and it asks:
- question `conflict:requirement:REV-2/R-4:stroke_mm`: *"Two strokes recorded for R-4 in REV-2: 576 (page 4) and 600 (page 1, after 'Weitere laden'). Open R-4 in REV-2 again and record which is the requirement itself."*

**How it gets settled:** the follow-up agent adds a third observation that says why it's right:

```json
{"value": {"bore_mm": 50, "stroke_mm": 576, "pressure_bar": 210, "mounting": "Schwenkauge", "certification": "none"},
 "verified": true,
 "reason": "Page 4 is R-4's own page; the appended row on page 1 repeats R-4 with an older value",
 "source": {"site": "customer-portal", "locator": "viewer REV-2, page 4", "agent": "spec-followup", "at": "06:05"}}
```

`resolve()` uses the verified observation, and the question disappears.

## 3. Messy values: raw text plus normalized value

```json
{"kind": "requirement", "key": "REV-2/R-1",
 "observations": [{
   "value": {
     "stroke_mm":     {"raw": "200 (en-US)",    "value": 200},
     "pressure_bar":  {"raw": "1.250 (de-DE)",  "value": 1250},
     "certification": {"raw": "Prüfvermerk siehe Freigabestand; tooltip: EN 1",  "value": "EN 1"}},
   "source": {"site": "customer-portal", "locator": "viewer REV-2, page 1", "agent": "spec"}}]}

{"kind": "revision", "key": "REV-3",
 "date":    {"raw": "11/01 (TT/MM) 2030", "value": "2030-01-11"},
 "marking": {"raw": "ersetzt", "value": "superseded"}}
```

**What code does with it:**
- It calculates only with `value`.
- **Validators recheck simple cases:** if `raw` carries a locale or format hint, code parses `raw` itself and compares. `"1.250 (de-DE)"` must give 1250, and `"11/01 (TT/MM)"` must give 11 January. If an agent wrote 1.25 or 1 November, the validator rejects the record, and the agent gets the error back and corrects it.
- Where code can't parse, like the tooltip text, `raw` stays for a human or model recheck.

## 4. Something the rules don't cover: an observation

```json
{"kind": "observation", "key": "obs-12",
 "about": {"kind": "position", "key": "4"},
 "text": "Position 4's unit is 'VE' (Verpackungseinheit), neither Stk nor Satz. No conversion to pieces found yet.",
 "quote": "Menge: 6 VE",
 "source": {"site": "tender-portal", "locator": "LV, row 4", "agent": "tender"}}
```

**`resolve()` says:** position 4 has `unit_kind: "other"`, so it's omitted, and
- question `unit:position:4`: *"Position 4 is in VE: find how many pieces one VE is (specification, data sheet, Q&A)."*
- the observation shows up in the orchestrator's list next to the question.

If an agent then finds "1 VE = 4 Stück", there's no field for it today. **That's the moment to extend the schema** (e.g. `pieces_per_unit` with the unit name), during development, not during the run.

## What the orchestrator then sees from `open_questions()`

```
verify:position:3:requirement           warning   Position 3 names no requirement. Check the tender documents …
conflict:requirement:REV-2/R-4:stroke   blocking  Two strokes recorded for R-4 in REV-2: 576 vs 600 …
unit:position:4                         blocking  Position 4 is in VE: find how many pieces one VE is …
observation obs-12                      info      Position 4's unit is 'VE' …
```

- **Blocking** questions prevent pricing the affected positions.
- **Warnings** allow pricing but deserve a check if there's time.
- **Info** is context for the orchestrator.

**The common pattern:** nothing is silently guessed. Every doubt stays visible in the store, with its source, until an agent settles it.

content.text:
`resolve()` doesn't infer anything. **The agent infers the link**, and `resolve()` only reads the label the agent put on it.

## Who does what

**The agent** (a model) writes the record. If the bill of quantities names no requirement for position 3, the model uses what's on the page and in the store, for example:
- the position's text: "Doppeltwirkender Zylinder für **Hubwerk**"
- the requirement titles the spec agent already saved: R-1 "Abstützung", R-2 "**Hubwerk**", R-4 "Verriegelung"
- technical details in the position text, if any ("bore 63 mm"), compared with the requirements' attributes

That's a judgment, which is why it's the model's job, not code's. It writes the result with `"basis": "inferred"` and its reasons.

**`resolve()`** only sees `basis: "inferred"` and turns it into the warning. It doesn't check whether the inference is good; it just makes sure it doesn't go unnoticed.

## Why the warning matters

The requirement decides the material, and the material decides price, lead time and quantity scales. A wrong link makes the whole position wrong, and with no_bid it could even flip the decision. Rule 2 also says "the requirement **referenced by** the position", so an inferred link is a fallback, not the intended route. That's why the verify question doesn't ask "is R-2 right?" but "**find the stated reference**". In public-1 it was there: the bill-of-quantities CSV and the position overview both named the requirement for each position.

## What code could still check deterministically

`resolve()` can't do the fuzzy text comparison itself. It could, though, check an inferred link for consistency:
- If the position text mentions numbers ("63 mm", "250 bar") and they contradict R-2's attributes, that becomes a **conflict** instead of just a warning.
- If two positions point to the same requirement and one of them is inferred, the inferred one gets a closer look.

So the split stays the same: the model makes the judgment, code makes sure every judgment is visible and checks whatever can be checked mechanically.

content.text:
It wouldn't. I made that part of the example up without saying so, and it doesn't hold for the real data.

**What I assumed:** that the specification gives each requirement a functional title like "Hubwerk". Then the agent could match "Zylinder für Hubwerk" in the position to the requirement titled "Hubwerk".

**What public-1 actually looks like** (from the other thread's real spec facts): the requirement table has the columns Referenz, Anforderung (original wording), Bohrung, Hub, Druck, Befestigung and Zertifizierung. The original wording reads like *"Bohrung 63 mm, Hub 489 mm, Betriebsdruck 250 bar, Befestigung Flansch, Zertifizierung EN 1493. Kataloggruppe GR-5152 …"*. There's no "Hubwerk" anywhere in the spec. The word only appears on the tender side, in the position texts. My schema has no title or wording field for requirements either.

**And it's a trap on public-1:** position 01.03 is called "Hydraulikzylinder **Verstellung**", but its description says *"für Hubwerk, gemäß Lastenheft Anforderung A-2"*. Matching by names would have led nowhere or to the wrong requirement. The stated reference "A-2" is what counts, and it was there.

**So when the reference is missing, inference only works if the evidence gives it a real basis:**
- **The spec states a purpose or title** for its requirements. Then a match by name is possible. To use it, the schema needs a field for the requirement's own wording; today it doesn't have one.
- **The position text contains technical values** ("bore 63 mm, 250 bar"). Then the agent can compare them with the requirements' attributes. That's the more reliable route, and code can check it.
- **Neither:** then there's no basis. The agent should **not guess** but leave `requirement` empty. `resolve()` then reports a blocking gap ("Position 3: find its requirement reference"), and the position isn't priced until the reference is found.

**What this means for the design:**
1. **Every inferred link must quote recorded evidence from both sides:** the position text *and* the spec text it matches. If one side can't be quoted, it isn't an inference but a guess.
2. **The schema needs the requirement's original wording**, so such a match can be quoted and rechecked at all.
3. **An inference is a last resort.** First the agent searches for the stated reference: bill-of-quantities file, position overview, Q&A. In public-1 the reference was stated for every position.

content.thinking:
The user is pushing on what happens if there's no link at all—isn't adaptive handling exactly where Claude Code should shine over a fixed schema? That's fair, but the store isn't competing with that adaptability; the agents themselves remain Claude Code, and the store plus resolver only handles the deterministic, structured part of the problem.

When a link is genuinely missing, the store surfaces a gap—like a blocking question asking for the requirement of position 3—and hands that off to the adaptive orchestrator, which can search other docs, infer with evidence, allow a partial submission, or flag a no-bid. Whatever judgment call it makes gets written back into the store as an explicit decision or override with justification, so the resolver can still apply it rather than stalling forever; essentially, resolve handles known rules while anything unresolved escalates as a question the orchestrator answers through evidence or deliberate judgment.

There's a fully adaptive alternative—let Claude Code do everything including computation—but that sacrifices arithmetic reliability, which is exactly where models tend to err. I'm thinking a hybrid works best: resolve handles the rule mechanics deterministically, while Claude Code could also independently compute the bid as a cross-check, flagging disagreements for investigation, with judgment records or a direct fallback computation as the escape hatch when rules don't fit the data.

Walking through the "no link" scenario concretely: the tender agent writes a null requirement with observation notes, resolve flags it as a blocking question, the orchestrator queries the spec and tender agents for more context, and if still unresolved, it either infers an attribute match or omits the position—recording either choice as a Judgment that resolve then applies and traces show clearly.

content.text:
Yes. Handling the unexpected is exactly what an adaptive agent is better at than a fixed schema. But that isn't a contradiction with the design, because **the orchestrator and the browser agents *are* adaptive Claude Code.** The store and `resolve()` only take over what's mechanical once the facts are settled. The question is where the boundary sits, and how the unexpected gets from code back to the adaptive part.

## The principle: code doesn't guess, it escalates

`resolve()` only applies rules it knows. Anything it can't settle, it doesn't decide. It turns it into a question for the orchestrator. The orchestrator, which is Claude Code, can answer in two ways:
1. **Find evidence:** send an agent to look somewhere else.
2. **Make a justified judgment** when there's really nothing to find, and **write that judgment into the store**.

The second way is the piece that's missing today: a `Judgment` record. With it, nothing stays blocked forever, and the adaptive decision is still visible and traceable.

## Walkthrough: position 3 really has no link

**1. The tender agent records what it saw, and what it didn't:**
```json
{"kind": "position", "key": "3", "quantity": {"raw": "16 Stk", "value": 16}, "unit_kind": "piece",
 "requirement": null}
{"kind": "observation", "about": {"kind": "position", "key": "3"},
 "text": "No requirement reference for position 3: not in the LV row, the LV file or the position overview."}
```

**2. `resolve()` escalates:** a blocking question `link:position:3:requirement`. Position 3 isn't priced.

**3. The orchestrator works on it like a person would:**
- It sends the tender agent to the Q&A ("did anyone ask about position 3?").
- It sends the spec agent: "Does the specification assign requirements to positions anywhere?"
- It compares what's known: position 3's text says "63 mm, 250 bar", and of all requirements only R-2 has those values.

**4. If there's still no stated link, the orchestrator decides and writes the decision down:**
```json
{"kind": "judgment", "about": {"kind": "position", "key": "3", "field": "requirement"},
 "choice": "R-2",
 "reason": "No reference anywhere (LV, overview, Q&A, spec checked). Position text states bore 63 mm and 250 bar; R-2 is the only requirement with both.",
 "evidence": ["position:3", "requirement:REV-2/R-2", "observation:obs-14"],
 "by": "orchestrator"}
```
If even that basis were missing, the judgment would be `"choice": "omit"`, meaning the position is left out of the bid, which the brief allows.

**5. `resolve()` applies the judgment** and notes it in the trace: `position 3: requirement R-2 by judgment (orchestrator): no reference found, values match`.

## Why not let Claude Code do everything?

It could. One Opus session that researches, decides and calculates would adapt to anything. But:
- **Rules 12–28 are where models slip:** withdrawn answers, the conditional threshold without falling back to older approvals, cent allocation with largest remainders, rounding at exactly the right step. Code gets those right every time.
- **Code makes the result checkable:** trace, tests, and the same output from the same evidence.

The split that gets you both:

| Situation | Who handles it |
|---|---|
| Known rule, facts available | `resolve()` |
| Facts missing | `resolve()` asks → orchestrator sends agents |
| Unexpected, no evidence findable | orchestrator decides → `Judgment` in the store → `resolve()` applies it |
| Something no rule covers | orchestrator writes an observation; during development, extend the schema |

**A useful addition:** a cross-check. Let the orchestrator calculate one or two positions itself, roughly, and compare with `compute_bid()`. A large difference doesn't decide anything, but it points to a wrong link or a misread value.

So adaptivity isn't lost; it's channeled. Claude Code handles everything that needs judgment and writes that judgment explicitly into the store, and code handles everything mechanical.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the premises against the data: all five positions link directly to their requirements (A-1 through A-5) with no inferred connections, and each requirement maps cleanly to a Kataloggruppe and material without gaps.

For the rules and relations, everything resolves correctly — withdrawal and amendment numbers, stroke reserves, the Satz conversion using pieces-per-set, FX conversions, metal index selection, condition groups, packaging, commitments, pool and bonus terms, and the conditional discount threshold — with no warnings raised, meaning the schema covers all relation types without needing extensions, and retrieval completed in a single pass with no gaps.

On the messiness/conflict premise, I can't fully verify it since the log doesn't track conflicts explicitly, though I do see the A-4 duplicate row (600 = 576 + 24) was resolved by using 576, suggesting the agent handled that conflict correctly.

Now checking some trickier cases: the 01.03 vs 01.02 lead-time discrepancy for HZ-2170 makes sense once I trace the pooled demand of 45 against each position's max commitment (44 vs 45) — 01.02 stays within commitment for a 3-week lead time while 01.03 exceeds it and falls back to the stock rule, producing 11 weeks, which matches the intended "commitment may differ by position" trap. Similarly, 01.01's 2-week lead time checks out since its commitment fails (25 > 24) but stock coverage kicks in, and 01.04/01.05 both stay within their commitment limits for 3 weeks. I'm now working through the 01.05 rebate calculation, tallying eligible goods across 01.03, 01.04, and 01.05 to get a total near 298,901.96, then applying the tiered bonus bands (2% up to 15000, 5% above) to check if the credit of 11,683.58 lines up.

I verify the total rebate sums correctly (580.41 + 2,131.11 + 11,683.58 = 14,395.10) and check the setup pool allocation by mass across 01.03–01.05, confirming the surcharge-per-unit math roughly holds. Then I turn to the submission timing and cost: retrieval took about 650 seconds in a single serial session, submission dragged on for 16–18 minutes against a 20-minute limit, and the retrieval cost ($5.36) compared to Atira's $3.68 so far suggests the serial approach is both slow and pricier — a point favoring parallelization. I also flag a concern that the submit agent repeatedly used an unsafe browser code-execution tool over multiple long calls, which isn't explicitly restricted but might indicate it's struggling with the configurator UI rather than a deliberate workaround.

I note the Playwright tools aren't allowlisted, so the cc-agent has access to the full toolset including unsafe code execution — worth flagging as an observation rather than a definite problem. There's also a minor model-alias warning that resolved fine since calls routed to the correct model, and confirmation that only one model call happens at a time, reinforcing the serial bottleneck. The cached token count (7.38M) implies each turn re-reads a large context, which supports the idea that per-agent smaller contexts would be cheaper, and the actual retrieval time (10.8 min) ran notably longer than the earlier 6–8 minute estimate. Since the submission run was still in progress when I last checked, I'm considering whether to check back shortly before finalizing my analysis.

content.text:
The run is still going: at 14:13 the submit agent was entering the bid, and there's no score yet. The research and the bid are complete, though, and they answer most of our premises.

**What ran:** `cc-agent` v1.3. One Opus session (via OpenRouter) did the retrieval and produced the evidence JSON, then `bid_engine.resolve()` computed the bid, then a submit session started entering it.

## The premises

| Premise | Holds? | What the log shows |
|---|---|---|
| **Links are stated in the data** (position → requirement) | ✅ yes | All 5 positions have a stated requirement (01.01 → A-1, 01.02 and 01.03 → A-2, 01.04 → A-4, 01.05 → A-5). Nothing had to be inferred; **0 warnings** |
| **Requirement → Kataloggruppe → material works** | ✅ yes | Every position found an exact, active material: HZ-1609, HZ-2170 (twice), HZ-3916, HZ-6932 |
| **The fixed schema covers every relation** | ✅ yes for public-1 | Every relation the rules name was resolved, see below. No position omitted, **0 gaps**, so the gap round wasn't needed |
| **`resolve()` handles the tricky rules correctly** | ✅ as far as I can check by hand | Bonus and delivery trap recomputed below; final score still pending |
| **Data is messy, conflicts must be kept** | ⚠️ can't tell from this log | The schema has no conflict tracking yet, so conflicts aren't visible. The known duplicate A-4 row was handled: the agent recorded 576 mm, which matches R-4's own page 4 in the other thread's earlier run |
| **One serial session is too slow and expensive** | ✅ confirmed | Retrieval took 650 s, 94 turns, with **at most 1 model call at a time**. About 7.4M cached input tokens means about 74K tokens of context per turn. That's $5.36 by Claude Code's estimate; Atira's metering showed $3.68 for the whole run at 14:13 |

**Every relation in the trace, resolved through the schema:**
- Withdrawn Q&A 8152 ignored; 01.05 = 26 Satz × 5 = **130 pieces** (pieces per set found)
- Amendment Q&A 8150: A-2 usable stroke 482, plus 2 × 9 reserve = 500
- A-4: 576 + 2 × 12 = 600
- USD conditions converted for HZ-2170 and HZ-3916
- Metal index chosen by date window (3.15 EUR/kg)
- Three different condition groups (base / none / base + surcharge)
- Packaging tariffs, delivery commitments, setup pool, bonus plan
- Conditional discount of 5 % with a threshold of 1 EUR

## Two checks that the rules really were applied

**1. The delivery trap.** 01.02 and 01.03 use the same material, HZ-2170, with different commitments: TZ-2832 (max 45) and TZ-4279 (max 44). Pooled demand is 29 + 16 = 45.
- 01.02: 45 ≤ 45, so the commitment applies: **3 weeks**
- 01.03: 45 > 44, so its commitment doesn't apply; stock doesn't cover the demand, so production: **11 weeks**

That's exactly rule 24: "A commitment may differ by position even for the same material."

**2. The project bonus.**
- Eligible goods value: 16 × 753.23 + 21 × 2,107.18 + 130 × 1,866.15 = 298,901.96 EUR
- Marginal bands: 2 % of the 10,000 between 5,000 and 15,000 = 200.00, plus 5 % of the 283,901.96 above 15,000 = 14,195.10
- Total: **14,395.10 EUR**
- Rebates in the bid: 580.41 + 2,131.11 + 11,683.58 = **14,395.10** ✓

## Two things that stand out

1. **Time is getting tight.** Retrieval took 10:54. Submission started at 10:55 and was still going at 14:13, on its fifth `browser_run_code_unsafe` call in a row, which suggests it's struggling with the bid form. Whether everything fits in 20 minutes will only show at the end. Parallel research would save the most here.
2. **The browser tools aren't restricted.** The agents use `browser_find` and `browser_run_code_unsafe`, a Playwright tool that runs arbitrary code. That isn't forbidden as such, but for the fair-play review and for predictability I'd use an allowlist of browser tools.

**Bottom line:** on public-1, the premises for the fixed schema and deterministic rules hold. Links were stated, every relation fit the schema, and the result had no gaps or warnings. Not verified by this run: whether the bid scores well (that comes with the result) and how the design copes with conflicts, which it doesn't track yet. Should I look at the score and the submission once the run is finished?

content.thinking:
It's reached step 9 (Erklärungen) of this multi-step wizard at 16:02, meaning it navigated through 8 prior steps despite the traps like the fake browser back button and the "back discards subsequent steps" warning. This submission is taking at least 5 minutes regardless, consistent with Qwen's 5.4 minute run to reach the TAN step.

The real bottleneck isn't missing context—the agent has the brief, bid, and logins—but rather unfamiliarity with the form's structure itself, which it has to discover step by step, snapshotting and filling each one via code execution that's slow to write. It also lost the retrieval session's prior login state, so it's likely re-encountering cookie walls and portal logins fresh, even though some browser tabs may have persisted. Ultimately, the submission wizard's sheer complexity—nine-plus steps with save-on-continue behavior—seems to be the core difficulty, more than turn latency or context size.

I'm thinking through possible fixes: starting submission prep earlier in parallel with retrieval for steps that don't depend on the bid, giving the submit agent generic (non-site-specific) knowledge of the form flow, switching to a faster model for the mechanical form-filling work, restricting tool choice to push faster interaction patterns, and considering how to hand off context between the retrieval and submission agents more efficiently.

The retrieval session already has the portal and mail logged in, and the submit agent reuses that browser state, so handoff itself seems fine. The real issue looks less like missing context and more like the form itself being long and trap-laden combined with Opus being slow per step via run_code — I count roughly 14 run_code_unsafe calls between 13:07 and 16:00 while still on step 9, suggesting it may be struggling or looping on a particular step, though without screenshots I can't pinpoint which one. I'm also aware there's a 20-minute window closing in around 16:09, so time pressure is becoming a factor too.

content.text:
Partly, but missing context isn't the main reason. I looked at the live screen: at 16:02, five minutes into the submission, the agent is on **step 9 ("Erklärungen")** of the bid form on the tender portal. So it's progressing, just slowly. Three things make it slow:

**1. The form itself is long and full of traps.**
- It's a wizard with at least 9 steps, plus requesting the TAN and signing.
- On the screenshot: *"Changes are only saved with 'Weiter'. Back discards the following steps."*
- There's a fake browser bar built into the page with its own ← link, so a wrong click throws away steps.
- The brief warns about more: unsaved entries are lost when the session expires, each new TAN request invalidates the previous one, the TAN is only valid for 5 minutes, and there's a final confirmation dialog.

That's a lot of steps no matter how smart the model is. Qwen in run #1 also needed 5.4 minutes to reach the TAN.

**2. Opus writes code for every step.** Since 13:07 the log shows about 15 calls to `browser_run_code_unsafe`: Opus writes a small Playwright script per action. Each of those turns took 7–35 seconds, because the model has to write the code first. For filling in a form, that's a slow way to work. A faster model with plain `fill_form` and `click` would probably move through the steps faster.

**3. It has the context it needs, but not the form's structure.** The submit session gets the brief's submission section, the calculated bid and the logins. The browser is still logged in from retrieval; the screenshot shows the retrieval tabs still open. What it doesn't know is what the form looks like, so it discovers it step by step with a snapshot of each page. The retrieval session never saw the form either, because it was told not to submit. So more context from retrieval wouldn't have helped much.

## What would help

1. **Start the parts that don't depend on the bid early, in parallel with research:** expressing interest ("Teilnahme bekunden") and registering the bidder (company name and USt-IdNr. are in the brief). Saves a few minutes. The risk is that the portal session expires while research is still running, so it needs a test.
2. **Use a faster model for the submit agent** (Sonnet or Haiku), and an allowlist of browser tools without `run_code_unsafe`. The form is mechanical work, not a reasoning task.
3. **Give it a generic procedure, not a site-specific one:** fill a step, save with "Weiter", never go back, request the TAN last, take the newest TAN mail. The prompt already contains most of this. A step list copied from the public portal wouldn't carry over to the private dataset's different software.

**Timing:** the run is at 16+ minutes. As a test run that doesn't matter, because test runs may last up to 2 hours. As a scored run with its 20-minute limit, this would be very tight: 10:54 for retrieval plus 5+ minutes of submitting, and it isn't done yet. So the order of fixes is: parallel research first (the biggest saving), then a faster submit agent.

content.thinking:
Right—I can't optimize for the specific form details like selectors, URLs, or exact button labels since those would be overfitting to public-1. But I can optimize for generic patterns that hold across any bid portal submission, since the brief states the jobs and answer format will stay consistent and each run's brief includes a submission section.

That means: reading the brief's own submission instructions at runtime, speeding things up independent of the form itself (faster model, batched fill_form calls, smaller context), following generic wizard discipline (save each step, never go back, use the latest valid TAN), starting prep early once bid-independent info is known, and adding a robustness check where the agent verifies the final summary matches the bid JSON before submitting. The answer schema itself is fixed regardless of the form—the configurator collects "exactly this answer"—so what gets entered is constant even though how it's entered varies, mirroring the same split seen in retrieval.

content.text:
Right. Optimizing for this particular form would be overfitting: the private dataset uses other software, so the step list, field names, buttons and the fake browser bar may all look different. But a lot can be optimized **without assuming anything about the form**. It's the same split as for research: what to enter is fixed, how the form looks is not.

## What's fixed, so you can rely on it

- **What gets entered.** The brief says the configurator collects exactly Atira's answer format, and the answer format is the same in the private dataset. So the values are always the same fields: reference, decision, discount, and per position the material, quantity, prices, lead time and breakdowns, plus the total.
- **The submission instructions arrive at runtime.** Every run's brief has its own submission section, describing *that* portal. The submit agent already gets it, so it adapts to the private portal automatically.
- **The basic mechanics of a signed online bid:** save each step before moving on, don't go back, request the TAN last, use only the newest TAN, confirm at the end. The public brief states these explicitly; a private brief will presumably describe its own equivalents.

## What you can optimize generically

| Optimization | Why it doesn't depend on the form |
|---|---|
| **A faster model for submitting** (Sonnet or Haiku instead of Opus) | Filling forms is mechanical on any portal; Opus writing Playwright code per step is slow anywhere |
| **A tool allowlist** (`fill_form`, `click`, `select_option`, snapshot) | `fill_form` fills several fields in one turn on any form |
| **Fresh, small context** | The submit session only needs the brief's submission section, the bid and the logins; no research history |
| **Start earlier / in parallel** | Expressing interest and registering the bidder don't depend on the bid. They exist in any tender process; whether the session survives that long has to be tested |
| **A guaranteed time slot** | Start the submission with enough time left, whatever the form looks like |
| **A check of the summary page** | The agent reads the summary back, and code compares it with the bid JSON. That catches typos on any form |

## What you shouldn't do

Hardcode step names, field labels, URLs or selectors from the public portal into prompts or code. That's overfitting, and copying values from the public sites into the package also risks the fair-play review.

**The biggest lever isn't the submission at all, it's retrieval:** 10:54 serial on one browser. Running research in parallel saves more time than any submit tweak, and it's just as independent of the form.
